title: Fourteen days: how Jensen Huang lost Nvidia, and what nobody has proved
dek: From the first report of a suspected Chinese spy to his resignation took two weeks. The affair is admitted. The espionage is not established, and the fight has moved to who may rent America's AI chips.
body:
Fourteen days passed between the first newspaper report and the resignation. On October 29, The New York Times reported that American officials had concluded a businesswoman close to Jensen Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset [1]. On November 12, Huang left Nvidia, the company he co-founded in 1993 and ran for 33 years, giving up both the chief executive's job and his board seat [2]. In between came a denial, an admission, a board inquiry, a second report about a second relationship, and a slide in the share price that carried the world's most valuable chipmaker below $4 trillion [2][9].

What did not arrive in those fourteen days is proof. The attorney general says the Justice Department has not concluded that the woman, Alice Huang, is a spy [4]. CNN reports that the intelligence gathered on her does not establish it and that officials disagree about how strong the evidence is [5]. Singapore questioned her and found too little to charge her [4]. Nobody has been charged with anything. This is an account of what is established, what is alleged, what is still unknown, and why the argument has already moved from one man's conduct to the rules on where American AI chips can go.

## The fortnight, in order

- **October 8.** President Trump awards Huang the National Medal of Science [12].
- **October 29.** The Times reports that U.S. agencies, after electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, believed she was passing information to Beijing, and that communications with an American later identified as Jensen Huang turned up in that surveillance [1]. The two are not related [13].
- **October 30.** Huang tells Bloomberg his dealings with her were business and normal [1]. China's Foreign Ministry calls the report unsubstantiated [8].
- **November 4.** The Republican chairs of the House China, Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees ask Huang for a closed-door briefing on November 18 [3][8].
- **November 6.** A second Times report describes a classified memo from the spring, reportedly overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, saying China's Ministry of State Security recruited her to get close to him [1][19].
- **November 8.** Huang emails employees that he was unfaithful to his wife. The board opens an independent inquiry and says it has "no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised" [6].
- **November 9.** The stock closes 4.27 percent lower [14]. Trump says the FBI is looking into it and predicts Huang will come through [1].
- **November 10.** The board hires Joon H. Kim, a former acting U.S. attorney in Manhattan, and the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to run the inquiry [15].
- **November 11.** The Times reports a second relationship, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reported to Huang; she could not be reached for comment [2][6]. Reuters reports the board is meeting to consider removing him [2].
- **November 12.** Huang resigns, effective immediately. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress becomes interim chief executive and Harvey Jones, a director since 1993, becomes the company's first board chair [2][6].

Nvidia gave no reason for the departure [2]. The second report matters to the sequence because it changed the question in front of the board. An affair with a customer's executive is a security and judgment problem. A reported relationship with a subordinate is a governance problem of the ordinary kind, the kind boards remove chief executives for [6].

## Three piles: established, alleged, unproved

**Established.** Huang says he was unfaithful to his wife [6]. Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was the central figure at Megaspeed, a Singapore company that became one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers [7]. The two appeared together at industry events, including a group dinner in Taipei on May 22, 2025, that was filmed [1]. U.S. agencies had her under electronic surveillance [1]. Singapore opened an investigation of Megaspeed in February 2025, questioned her and withheld her passport that year [4].

**Alleged.** That the Ministry of State Security recruited her to cultivate Huang, that she passed information to Beijing, and that part of the purpose was to make Nvidia's advanced chips easier for China to get [1][4]. These claims come from people briefed on classified material, speaking to the Times without their names attached. Beijing rejects them [4]. Megaspeed says claims about its business are not backed by verifiable evidence [4].

**Unproved.** Whether she is a spy at all. Attorney General Todd Blanche said on November 12 that his department had not reached that conclusion [4]. Asked the same day, Trump answered: "I don't know if that's been determined yet" [4]. CNN, citing multiple sources, reported that the intelligence does not prove she acted for Beijing and that officials are split on the strength of the evidence [5]. Singapore concluded there was not enough to show she had committed a crime, though it suspected she gave inaccurate information to play down her role [4]. And nothing public shows that Huang knew of any intelligence tie, or that a company secret left the building [1][2].

One more fact sits awkwardly across all three piles. By the Times's account, Trump was briefed on the intelligence in 2025 and the memo circulated among senior officials last spring, yet Huang received the country's top science honor in October [1][12]. Who in government knew what, and whether anyone warned Nvidia, is now a question for Congress as much as for the board.

## The company in the middle

Megaspeed began as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer, incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International [4]. In March 2023 its shares moved to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company carrying Alice Huang's Chinese name, and it was renamed [4]. By November 2023 she was no longer listed as a director and her shares had passed to an entity owned by a Singaporean businessman, James Tan [4]. That same month Megaspeed joined an Nvidia partner program [1].

Then it grew at a rate that is hard to picture. Singapore filings show total assets rising about 90-fold in a year, to almost $3 billion by the end of 2024 [4]. Trade records cited by the Times show a Malaysian sister company buying at least $4.8 billion of equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, about 136,000 graphics processors [8]. Reporters who went looking for the people behind those purchases found a locked door at the Singapore headquarters, a rent-by-the-day office in Sydney whose listed director sells newspapers hundreds of miles away, and a run-down storefront outside Kuala Lumpur [7].

Megaspeed says Alice Huang left on August 30, 2025, and has no role [4]. A short seller, Culper Research, quoted an employee in May saying she was still the boss [4]. The company says it "conducts legitimate and lawful business," that inspections by the U.S. Commerce Department found no illicit transfers, and that it has hired outside lawyers to investigate [7][8].

American interest in Megaspeed is older than the scandal. The Commerce Department began examining it in late 2024, and a department official saw Nvidia equipment still in its boxes at a Malaysian data center [1]. In August 2025, Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, contacted Commerce investigators about the case; afterward the Justice Department asked Commerce to pause and opened a criminal inquiry of its own [1]. Senator Tom Cotton asked for a formal investigation that October [10]. Lawmakers had asked Nvidia as early as April 2025 for a list of big chip buyers across Southeast Asia [11].

## The loophole underneath

The export rules that matter here control where a chip is shipped. They say much less about who rents time on it. A Chinese company that cannot buy Nvidia's best processors can, in many cases, lease computing power from a data center in Malaysia that can. That is the business Megaspeed was in, and it is why the case has become an argument about law rather than about one executive.

The House passed a bill in January, the Remote Access Security Act, that would extend export controls from the physical chip to cloud access, barring Chinese firms from renting servers built on advanced Nvidia chips in third countries; it is waiting in the Senate [8]. Nvidia's own rule requires cloud customers to sell at least 51 percent of their capacity to companies outside China, but only on new contracts [8]. Oracle recently dropped a five-year, $7 billion plan to lease up to 100,000 advanced chips' worth of capacity in Southeast Asia to Tencent after U.S. officials objected, according to the Financial Times as summarized by Asia Times [8].

Huang was the industry's most effective voice against tighter limits. Trump approved sales of Nvidia's H200 chips to China in December 2025, with inspections, shipment caps and a 25 percent levy, after Huang pressed the case [1][2]. That is why the allegation, if it were ever proved, would carry weight beyond the company: the suspected aim was to influence the man who was influencing the policy [1]. It is also why the absence of proof matters. His argument that controls push China to build its own chips is one he made in public for years, long before any of this [2].

## The price

Investors had started selling before the scandal. Nvidia peaked near $240 on October 5 and was already sliding [16]. It closed at $186.64 on Friday, November 6, the last session before the admission [20]. The fortnight turned a slide into a rout.

::: chart Nvidia's closing share price, the week Huang left
| Close, in dollars
Fri. Nov. 6 | 186.64 | $186.64
Mon. Nov. 9 | 178.67 | $178.67
Wed. Nov. 11 | 173.73 | $173.73
Thu. Nov. 12 | 166.19 | $166.19
Fri. Nov. 13 | 162.85 | $162.85
note: Nov. 9 is the Nov. 6 close less the 4.27 percent fall CNBC reported; Nov. 13 is the Nov. 12 close less the 2.01 percent fall CNBC reported; the others are closes as published. Tuesday Nov. 10 is left out because no close for it was read. On Thursday the stock fell as much as 14 percent before recovering.
:::

Wednesday's close was $173.73 and Thursday's $166.19 [3][16]. The week's loss was 12.75 percent, the sixth weekly decline in a row and the longest such run since 2012 [9]. Over those six weeks the company shed roughly $1.6 trillion in value and dropped behind Apple [17]. Huang's own stake, 3.6 percent of the company, was valued at about $150 billion when he left [6].

The business has not visibly weakened. Revenue in the first half of the fiscal year was $96 billion, up 85 percent, and the company controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for advanced AI chips [2][6]. What the fall measures is how much of Nvidia's value was attached to one person. The company had no board chair, no chief operating officer and no announced succession plan until the morning he resigned [6].

## Washington moves in

Congress did not wait for the board. On the day Huang resigned, the three House chairs asked him for a closed, transcribed interview on December 1 and Teter for one on December 2, with subpoenas threatened if they declined; one of the chairs, Brian Mast, told reporters Huang had agreed to brief lawmakers [3]. Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott asked Huang to testify in public on December 3 and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on December 10, writing: "The American people deserve answers" [3]. Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons asked Lutnick, Rubio and the White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, to preserve records on Nvidia's China exports [3].

The House chairs also want four chip security bills attached to the annual defense bill [3]. Democrats, who won both chambers on November 3, have been asking for much the same thing [8]. This is one of the few subjects on which the two parties are pulling in one direction.

Inside the administration the tone is less settled. Trump defended Huang throughout and, after the resignation, suggested Tim Cook as successor with the line "A Legend replaces a Legend"; Cook left Apple's top job in September and has shown no interest [2]. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that whether Alice Huang is a spy does not matter to him; what matters is whether Nvidia had a culture of complying with export law, and he urged the board to hire from outside [4]. China's Foreign Ministry warned on Friday that tighter chip controls would threaten supply chains [3].

## The case for each reading

There are two honest ways to read these fourteen days, and the evidence does not yet choose between them.

**The security reading.** A foreign service does not need a recruit to steal blueprints. Access to the thinking of the one executive who talks to the president about chip policy is valuable on its own. On this view the unanswered spy question is beside the point: a chief executive with a concealed relationship to the leader of a customer under federal investigation was exposed to pressure, and the company's controls failed to notice a multibillion-dollar buyer with empty offices [7]. Bessent's remark is a version of this [4].

**The due-process reading.** A man lost his company on the strength of anonymous descriptions of classified material that the government's own lawyers decline to endorse [4][5]. The accused woman has not been heard from; the Associated Press could not reach her, and Al Jazeera reported her whereabouts unknown [4][13]. Megaspeed has passed the inspections it was given [8]. And the leak landed in the middle of a live policy fight, which is a reason for care about who benefits from the story being told this way. Beijing's dismissal of the whole account as a smear is self-interested, but the request for evidence is not unreasonable [4].

Both can be partly right. The resignation is fully explained by what Huang admitted and by the second report. The national security case is not explained by anything yet made public.

## What to watch

- **November 17.** Nvidia reports quarterly results after the close, the first call Kress leads as interim chief. The board says it is choosing a search firm [18].
- **December 1 to 10.** The House interviews of Huang and Teter, the Senate hearing with Huang, and Lutnick's testimony [3].
- **The board's inquiry.** Kim and Wachtell have no public deadline, and the board has not said whether findings will be released [15].
- **The Justice Department.** A criminal inquiry into Megaspeed has been open since August 2025 [1]. A charge, or a decision not to bring one, would do more to settle the central question than anything said so far.
- **The Senate.** Whether the remote-access bill, or the four bills the House chairs want in the defense package, moves before the new Congress is seated [3][8].
- **Megaspeed's customers.** Who was renting the 136,000 processors, and from where, is the fact that would show whether a loophole was used or merely existed [8].

Jensen Huang built the company that the AI boom runs on and lost it in two weeks. The first of those weeks was about a spy story that remains unproved. The second was about conduct he admitted. The part that will outlast both is duller and larger: a rule written for boxes of chips, in a world where computing is rented by the hour.
